structured_output.summary: The most useful new evidence comes from the 2026 Fable/Fulcrum CIFAR-10 record, 1.74–1.83 s against Hiverge's 1.98 s. It used progressive resizing, but differently from E013 in three ways. It bilinearly downsampled the whole image instead of taking 24 px random crops. It ran three stages of 3 epochs each at 24, 28 and 32 px. And it added epochs, 8.875 against Hiverge's 7.65. Net saving was about 10% (−0.128 s from the 28→32 stage, then −0.081 s more from adding 24 px). So E013's −0.8 pp may reflect its crop-based setup rather than the idea, and H2.3 deserves a retest. Hiverge's 1.98 s recipe adds several other things the tree hasn't tried. It applies per-image brightness/contrast jitter (±0.14 / ±0.13). It renormalizes the Muon weights only periodically, every 2 steps at the start rising to every 17 by the end. It uses batch size 1536, and airbench94_muon uses 2000; our recipe uses 1024. Hiverge, Fable and airbench94_muon all train the whitening bias only briefly, for 0.2–3 epochs, and Fable has a separate no-whiten-bias-grad graph variant. Two other results back the tree's current reading. Fable's lr floor (0.05) with a short EMA tail matches E025's finding that a non-zero floor helps. Its CUDA graphs plus fused optimizer came out about 0.04 s slower than plain torch.compile, which fits E005 and the refuted H2.2. Literature on cheaper Muon orthogonalization (cubic Newton-Schulz, Turbo-Muon) promises only ~3% savings, less than the NS3 batching already done. One public CIFAR-100 submission reports that Muon lost to SGD, which conflicts with E014/E016. Its lookahead setup is unknown, so it is weak evidence against H1.2.

findings.claim: The Fable CIFAR-10 record (94% in 1.828 s; champion file e1_1.74s) uses a resolution curriculum of 24,24,24,28,28,28,32,32,32 px, one entry per epoch. Each image is bilinearly downsampled with F.interpolate(mode='bilinear'), not cropped ('downsample the whole scene, don't crop a window'). Total epochs rose from 7.65 to 8.875 (lr decay over 8.5 epochs), yet time still fell. The 28→32 curriculum saved 0.128 s and adding the 24 px stage saved another 0.081 s, about 10% net on a ~2 s run. Each resolution gets its own warmed-up compiled graph (no dynamic shapes), and the last full-res epochs 're-adapt BN stats'.
findings.relevance: E013 used 24 px random crops for the first 35% of epochs at the same epoch count and lost 0.8 pp. Fable's version differs on three axes: whole-image resize instead of crop, an intermediate 28 px stage, and extra epochs. So E013 does not refute progressive resizing as Fable does it. A 3-stage resize curriculum with ~+15% epochs is a concrete untested variant. Caveat: the CIFAR-10 gain may shrink on CIFAR-100, which needs finer detail.

findings.claim: Hiverge's 1.98 s CIFAR-10 record adds per-image GPU colour jitter. Brightness shift is U(-1,1)*0.1399 added and contrast is 1+U(-1,1)*0.1308 multiplied, both per-sample [B,1,1,1], inside a compiled function. The blog says it led to 'improved validation accuracies' but gives no number. Label smoothing is 0.09.
findings.relevance: This is a direct template for H1.8.1. The jitter costs two elementwise ops per batch, which is negligible. The effect size is unpublished, and the best values were tuned for CIFAR-10 at ~7.65 epochs.

findings.claim: Both Hiverge and Fable renormalize Muon weights only periodically, with norm_freq = 2 + int(15*progress). That is every 2 steps at the start and every 17 by the end, instead of every step as in airbench94_muon. Muon settings are lr 0.205–0.2255, momentum 0.655, Nesterov, 3 NS steps.
findings.relevance: Muon still costs ~1.43 ms/step after E023, about 9% of the step. Skipping the weight-norm projection on most steps removes part of that cost with recipe-tested safety. Their Muon lr and momentum also sit close to our tip (lr 0.16–0.24, momentum 0.6–0.8), consistent with E024/E026 finding a flat optimum there.

findings.claim: Muon-based CIFAR speedruns use larger batches than our 1024: Hiverge and Fable use 1536, airbench94_muon uses 2000, and wd is scaled with batch size (Hiverge 1.0418e-6*bs; airbench 2e-6*bs). Muon critical-batch-size analysis (arXiv 2507.01598) finds Nesterov momentum shifts the critical batch size up, and Muon keeps data efficiency at large batch.
findings.relevance: Batch size is not in the tree. With Muon, the per-step optimizer and lookahead overhead is paid per step, so bs 1536 cuts steps per epoch by a third. Larger GEMMs may also run more efficiently. This is a new direction: bs 1536 with wd/lr rescaled and epochs re-knee'd.

findings.claim: The whitening-layer bias is trained only early: for 3 of 8 epochs in airbench94_muon, 0.2 epochs in Hiverge (whiten_bias_grad = step < whiten_bias_train_steps), and 3 of 45 epochs in airbench96_faster. Afterwards it is frozen in a separate compiled graph variant; Fable keys its CUDA graphs on (resolution, whiten_bias_grad).
findings.relevance: If the tip still trains the whitening bias for the whole run, the backward pass computes the gradient through block 1's first conv at full resolution on every step. Freezing the bias after ~0.2–3 epochs is a nearly free systems/recipe change with precedent. The size of the saving is unmeasured; a guess is a few percent.

findings.claim: Fable's lr decays linearly to a floor of 0.05x, not zero, followed by a half-epoch 'stabilization tail' at low lr. During that tail it keeps a lookahead-style weight EMA (decay 0.7 every 4 steps, starting 8 steps before decay ends), and BN buffers are not averaged. The EMA paper (2411.18704) finds that EMA needs less aggressive lr decay than last-iterate SGD, and that BN statistics must be recomputed for long averaging windows.
findings.relevance: This corroborates E025 (decay-to-zero hurt with lookahead) and E012. The tail shape is a lever only in the floor-up direction. It also points to an untested idea: recompute BN statistics for the averaged weights with a short timed forward pass over training batches.

findings.claim: Fable captured the whole run as one CUDA graph with a fused foreach optimizer. Retimed fairly against plain torch.compile on the same curriculum, the full stack was ~0.04 s slower. It also replaced MaxPool/AdaptiveMaxPool with a global x.flatten(2).max(2), which is bit-identical and avoids a slow atomic backward. This pool change is needed at 24 px, where the feature map is 2x2.
findings.relevance: This supports the refutation of H2.2/H2.2.1 (launch and optimizer overhead is not where time goes) and matches E010. If resizing is tried, note that the tip's F.max_pool2d(x, 4) assumes a 4x4 final map, and amax had an Inductor NaN bug (E009). Low-res stages need flatten().max or per-resolution kernel sizes, checked with debug_nan.

findings.claim: Muon training quality is largely decoupled from how precisely the polar factor is computed. A 5-step cubic iteration (10 matmuls) matches 5-step quintic within ~1e-3 loss on LLMs. Turbo-Muon (AOL preconditioning) removes 1 of 5 NS iterations for ~3% end-to-end on speedrun benchmarks with no quality loss. Polar Express uses per-iteration minimax quintic coefficients and converges faster.
findings.relevance: After E023 the NS matmuls cost only ~0.15–0.2 ms/step, so 2 NS steps or Turbo/Polar-Express coefficients can save at most ~1%. That is low priority next to periodic normalization or batch size.

findings.claim: airbench96_faster scores each batch with a proxy model (widths 32/64/64, depth 2, trained the same 45 epochs at bs 1024). It keeps the 512 highest-loss examples of every 1024-example batch, i.e. 50%, for the main model, cutting time from 34.7 s to 27.3 s at 96%. The whitening bias is trained for 3 epochs.
findings.relevance: The filtering gain comes from a 45-epoch regime where a tiny proxy is cheap relative to the run. At 6.5 epochs, with 100 classes and only 500 images per class, a proxy is relatively expensive and dropping half of each batch is risky. This keeps H1.4 at low prior. The H1.4.1 self-scoring variant still pays the full forward pass.

findings.claim: Applied to CIFAR-100 without retuning, airbench96 reaches 79.76% with Cutout and 79.27% without. In airbench94 ablations, each feature's removal costs epochs: whitening is the biggest (21 vs 45 epochs), dirac init ~3.8, BN-bias lr scaling ~1.7, lookahead ~1.5, TTA ~1.2, alternating flip ~1.1.
findings.relevance: These are base rates for which inherited components matter. The 64x BN-bias lr is worth ~1.7 epochs on CIFAR-10 and was never retuned for CIFAR-100 or the Muon base, so it is a possible H1.7-style sweep target.

findings.claim: A public CIFAR-100 speedrun submission (75.29% in 8.11 s on a Modal A100) reports that 'Muon lost to SGD at every size' and dropped it. Its final recipe is 128/384/576, LS 0.3, lr 9, wd 0.012, 8.5 epochs, chosen from ~40 configs, with ~95% of GPU time in conv/BN/GELU kernels.
findings.relevance: This conflicts with E014/E016–E027, where Muon gave +1.3 pp. Their Muon setup is unknown (possibly without lookahead, which E020 shows costs ~0.9 pp, or untuned lr). It is weak external evidence against H1.2 and is outweighed by our paired results.

findings.claim: A critical-damping momentum schedule, mu(t)=1-2*sqrt(alpha(t)), reaches 90% on CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 2.34x faster but costs 0.46 pp final accuracy. On CIFAR-100 the final cost grows to 1.7 pp and the matched-accuracy speedup shrinks to 1.14x.
findings.relevance: Momentum scheduling gains shrink on CIFAR-100, so it is low priority as an H1.7-style knob.

findings.claim: The public repo README now describes official judging on an NVIDIA L40S 48GB with 50 organizer-selected seeds, a 75% mean, and a 59.30 s baseline. The repo has 0 pull requests and no public leaderboard.
findings.relevance: The judging hardware and seed count here differ from task.md (A100 80GB PCIe, 40 seeds), so the rules may have changed. Treat task.md as authoritative. Systems gains tuned on the A100 (autotune choices, H2.5) may not transfer to other judge hardware, which strengthens H4's case for keeping accuracy margin.
